clue.text: Seventh-heaven concerto, by George!

definitions.meaning: a state of ecstasy (a rhapsody) up in the sky
Gershwin's famous piece for piano and orchestra, composed by George Gershwin

explanation.walkthrough: 'by George!' looks like a mild oath; it names the composer George Gershwin. The first reading takes rhapsody as rapture and blue as the sky, i.e. heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: Gershwin's jazz-inflected work for piano and orchestra bears this title, and rapture in the sky reads as bliss on high.

clue.text: A captive one provokes heaven's wrath

definitions.text: A captive one provokes heaven's wrath

parts.words: A captive one provokes heaven's wrath
parts.note: recalls William Blake's line that a caged ... songbird puts all heaven in a rage

explanation.walkthrough: Blake's Auguries of Innocence: 'A Robin Redbreast in a Cage / Puts all Heaven in a Rage'. The clue paraphrases the couplet.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's couplet names this small garden bird as the caged creature that enrages heaven.

clue.text: Cynara, I could eat you!

parts.note: Cynara is the botanical genus of a thistle-like vegetable eaten for its fleshy bracts, and also a woman's name from Dowson's poem

explanation.walkthrough: Cynara sounds like a sweetheart addressed in a love poem (Ernest Dowson's 'Cynara'); it is the plant genus of the edible globe vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: The globe vegetable belongs to the genus Cynara, so it is something one could eat.

clue.text: Like Lady Macbeth washing her hands

definitions.text: Like Lady Macbeth washing her hands

parts.words: Like Lady Macbeth washing her hands
parts.note: in the sleepwalking scene of Macbeth, Lady Macbeth rubs her hands as if washing them while asleep

explanation.walkthrough: In Act 5 Scene 1 of Macbeth, Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep, rubbing at imagined blood on her hands.
explanation.definitionFit: She performs the hand-washing while walking in her sleep, which is the sleepwalking adjective.

clue.text: "Pipe to the spirit ——- of no tone' (Keats)

definitions.text: "Pipe to the spirit ——- of no tone' (Keats)

parts.words: "Pipe to the spirit ——- of no tone' (Keats)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Ode on a Grecian Urn, where unheard melodies are piped to the spirit

explanation.walkthrough: Keats, Ode on a Grecian Urn: 'Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear'd, / Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone'. The missing word completes the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote of little songs, unheard, played to the spirit; the plural for simple songs fills the gap.

clue.text: Occupying a farm as locum?

definitions.note: an adverb phrase: acting as a substitute

parts.note: being in a place means occupying it
a stead or steading is a farm and its buildings, as in homestead

explanation.surface: A temporary stand-in doctor lodges on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A locum is a doctor or priest standing in for another; 'as locum' means in someone's place.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum serves in place of another, so acting as one is doing something as a substitute.

clue.text: See 1
Plain reverse on everyone in South America

indicators.note: reverse tells us to turn the words on and everyone backwards as one run

parts.note: everyone means all

explanation.surface: A traveller in South America heads back across the flat country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverse' turns ON ALL into LLANO. 'in South America' places the plain: llanos are the grassy plains of Venezuela and Colombia.
explanation.definitionFit: A llano is a treeless grassland plain of northern South America.

clue.text: Makes unfriendly sets, perhaps, keep out of shooting distance

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so the shuffled letters hold the next piece inside
perhaps hints that sets is only one arrangement of its letters, so they are shuffled

parts.note: the range of a gun is its shooting distance

explanation.surface: Someone who alienates people keeps them beyond the reach of a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sets' looks like a noun for groups of people; it is anagram fodder signalled by 'perhaps'. 'keep' holds the gun's reach inside the shuffle; 'out of' is only surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to drive them apart and turn them cold, causing estrangement.

clue.text: One's pedigree on a passport? It's a thing that's growing

definitions.meaning: a voyager's family tree, the lineage of someone travelling abroad
a Madagascan plant related to the banana whose leaf bases hold water

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is a family tree belonging to a traveller; the second is a real plant, Ravenala, that grows in Madagascar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ravenala, a fan-shaped Madagascan plant, is named for travellers drinking the water stored in its leaves; a family tree is a pedigree.

clue.text: There's standing room here, out of the wet

definitions.text: There's standing room here, out of the wet

parts.words: There's standing room here, out of the wet
parts.note: a theatre-style phrase for the spot where you stand after climbing out of the tub

explanation.walkthrough: 'standing room' suggests a crowded theatre or bus; it is the small rug you stand on after a bath, just out of the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The absorbent rug placed beside the tub is where a bather stands on stepping out.

clue.text: " Those antique times In which the sword was —— unto right" (Spenser)

definitions.text: Those antique times In which the sword was —— unto right" (Spenser)

parts.words: Those antique times In which the sword was —— unto right" (Spenser)
parts.note: a gap-fill from The Faerie Queene, where the sword attended justice

explanation.walkthrough: Spenser's Faerie Queene, Book V: 'those antique times, In which the sword was servant unto right'. The missing word completes the line.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem the sword was an attendant or helper to justice, one who serves.

clue.text: Olympian dessert

parts.note: the gods of Olympus drank nectar, and a smooth-skinned peach bears a name built on that drink

explanation.walkthrough: Nectar was the drink of the gods on Mount Olympus; the fruit's name starts with that word.
explanation.definitionFit: The smooth-skinned peach variety, eaten as a dessert fruit, takes its name from the drink of the gods.

clue.text: A blooming lass, or bowed

definitions.meaning: a girl's name that is also a garden flower of the violet family, like Shakespeare's heroine in Twelfth Night
a stringed instrument played with a bow, pitched below the violin

explanation.walkthrough: 'or' joins the two readings.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both a pansy-like flower and a girl's name, and the tenor member of the string family played with a bow.

clue.text: A lozenge to end catarrh O medical man!

indicators.note: the end of the word catarrh supplies its closing pair of letters

parts.note: MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A patient with a cough begs a doctor for a throat sweet to cure it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lozenge' looks like a throat sweet; it is the diamond shape. 'to end' takes the last two letters of catarrh, RH; then O as printed and MB.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a lozenge is a diamond, an equal-sided parallelogram, which is a rhombus.

clue.text: See 1 down
A receptacle peculiar to the Riding

definitions.text: A receptacle peculiar to the Riding

parts.words: A receptacle peculiar to the Riding
parts.note: the Riding suggests a Yorkshire district, but here means horse riding and a pouch slung from a seat

explanation.walkthrough: The Ridings were the old divisions of Yorkshire, so 'peculiar to the Riding' sounds regional; it means a bag used in horse riding.
explanation.definitionFit: A pouch slung across a horse's back or a bicycle seat is a bag used when riding.

clue.text: Apollo, well up, with a good view all round

definitions.meaning: the famous Vatican statue of the god is the Apollo of this name

definitions.text: well up, with a good view all round
definitions.meaning: a raised turret or summerhouse built to command a view

explanation.walkthrough: The Apollo Belvedere is a celebrated marble statue in the Vatican's Belvedere courtyard; the word itself is Italian for 'fine view'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vatican courtyard that houses the Apollo statue shares its name with a high gazebo commanding a fine prospect.

clue.text: The Director General's got outside water supply in the houses

indicators.note: got outside means the outer letters surround what follows

parts.note: DG is Director General, and the possessive adds an S
a well is a source of water
taken as written

explanation.surface: The BBC chief has his own water source piped into the homes.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' after 'supply' gives letters rather than linking, which leaves 'the houses' as the definition; 'got outside' wraps the Director General's abbreviation around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Homes and residences are places where people dwell.

clue.text: Head on a trunk?

parts.note: head is slang for the nut, and a trunk is a tree, so a nut on a tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head on a trunk' pictures a body; nut is slang for the head and trunk is a tree trunk, so it is a tree that bears nuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A hazel or similar tree bears nuts, the slang word for a head, on its trunk.

clue.text: Non-commissioned painter ? Far from it

parts.note: a non-commissioned officer is a sergeant, but the portraitist of that sounding name worked constantly on commission

explanation.walkthrough: John Singer Sargent's name sounds like 'sergeant', a non-commissioned rank; yet as a society portraitist he was constantly commissioned.
explanation.definitionFit: John Singer Sargent, the American portrait painter, lived on commissioned portraits.

clue.text: Less than 4 feet is Bell: of Haworth

definitions.note: the forename of a pen name

parts.note: an ell is an old cloth measure of 45 inches, just under four feet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A short person called Bell lives in a Yorkshire village.
explanation.walkthrough: Emily Brontë, of Haworth in Yorkshire, wrote as Ellis Bell; the definition is the first part of that pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Brontë published Wuthering Heights under the pseudonym Ellis Bell while living at Haworth parsonage.

clue.text: The Brie's getting fruity

definitions.note: an adjective for a noun: a genus of fruit bushes

indicators.note: getting signals the cheese's letters becoming something else, a change of form

parts.note: read as Brie plus S, the 's standing for 'is' and giving its letter

explanation.surface: A ripe Brie starts to taste of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' rearranges BRIES into RIBES. Ribes is the botanical genus of currants and gooseberries, so 'fruity' points at fruit bushes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ribes is the plant genus of currants and gooseberries, bushes grown for fruit.

clue.text: Expletive old earl?

definitions.meaning: the oath 'by God', run together as one word
the Norman family of that name were medieval earls of Norfolk

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is an old oath, 'by God'; the second is the Bigod family, Earls of Norfolk in the Middle Ages.
explanation.definitionFit: The oath 'by God' written as one word matches the surname of the medieval Norfolk earls.

clue.text: They've got the push

parts.note: 'got the push' sounds like being sacked, but here means people with drive who shove forward

explanation.walkthrough: 'got the push' usually means dismissed; here it means having push, that is thrust and drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushy, ambitious go-getters have plenty of drive and forcefulness.

clue.text: The week-end is to the House a novel enough situation

parts.note: Sat, short for Saturday, is the end of the working week
taken as written

explanation.surface: A weekend at the stately home makes a pleasant setting for a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Satis is Latin for 'enough', and Satis House is Miss Havisham's home in Dickens's Great Expectations, which explains 'to the House a novel ... situation'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for sufficient, used in English as an adverb meaning adequately, is satis.

clue.text: More annoyed that the earring is broken

indicators.note: something broken comes apart, so the letters of earring are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is crosser still because her earring has snapped.
explanation.definitionFit: Crosser and more irate both mean more irritated.

clue.text: Pledge of dramatic importance

definitions.meaning: ... money is a deposit given as a pledge of good faith
Wilde's play The Importance of Being ...

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense refers to Oscar Wilde's comedy The Importance of Being Earnest.
explanation.definitionFit: A token deposit is an earnest of good faith, and Wilde's play pairs importance with being this.

clue.text: Edwardian haymakers?

definitions.meaning: Teddy boys, 1950s youths dressed in Edwardian-style suits
to ted is to spread out mown grass to dry, so those who do it

explanation.walkthrough: Teds were British youths of the 1950s who wore Edwardian-style drape jackets; 'ted' is also a farming verb for turning hay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Teddy boys aped Edwardian dress, and tedders spread hay to dry.

clue.text: "Let —— my strong enforcement be" (As You Like It)

definitions.text: "Let —— my strong enforcement be" (As You Like It)

parts.words: "Let —— my strong enforcement be" (As You Like It)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Orlando's speech in the forest, where he asks that mildness be his compulsion

explanation.walkthrough: As You Like It, Act 2 Scene 7: Orlando says 'Let gentleness my strong enforcement be', asking kindly rather than by force.
explanation.definitionFit: Orlando hopes mildness and kindness, rather than force, will win him food for Adam.
